title: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & the METHANE Report
learningObjectives: Perform the first-arriving crew's actions without getting pulled into patient care.
Apply CSCATTT as the order of MCI priorities.
Deliver a complete METHANE report in under 60 seconds.
Use plain-language radio and structured follow-up updates (CAN).

summary.title: The First Crew's Job Is Not Treatment
summary.content: The first ambulance sets the tone for the entire incident. The most common failure is the first crew treating the first patient they reach — the scene then runs without command for 20 minutes. First-due rule: one crew member takes COMMAND and the radio; the other does a rapid RECON/global triage. You stay visible, stay with the vehicle/command point, and you do not disappear into a patient.

summary.title: Safety 1-2-3: Self → Scene → Survivors
summary.content: Stop short. Park upwind, uphill, upstream, out of the traffic lane and away from obvious hazards (fuel, wires, smoke, crowds, unstable structure). Look for clues of CBRNE or violence: multiple people down without trauma, odd odors or clouds, dead animals, repeated blasts, gunfire. If it smells, looks, or feels wrong — withdraw and report. A dead or injured rescuer converts a resource into a patient.

summary.title: CSCATTT — The Order of Business
summary.content: Command & Control → Safety → Communication → Assessment → Triage → Treatment → Transport. The first four (CSCA) are MANAGEMENT; the last three (TTT) are MEDICAL SUPPORT. You cannot do TTT well until CSCA is in place. It's a priority list, not a pause — in reality you do several at once, but if something must slip, it's treatment, never command or safety.

summary.title: METHANE: The Universal First Report
summary.content: M — Major incident DECLARED (or 'standby'). E — EXACT location (grid/address, landmarks, which side). T — TYPE of incident (what happened: RTC, explosion, collapse, chemical). H — HAZARDS present and potential (fire, fuel, chemical, structural, violence, weather). A — ACCESS and egress routes (best approach, RV point, staging). N — NUMBER, severity and type of casualties (estimate: 'approx 25: 5 red, 8 yellow, 12 green'). E — EMERGENCY services present and REQUIRED (who's on scene, what you need). Short, factual, estimates are fine — a fast 80%-right report beats a slow perfect one.

summary.title: Radio Discipline
summary.content: Plain language, no 10-codes (NIMS standard — mutual-aid units won't share your codes). Name the incident ('Riverside Bus Command') so every unit knows who to call. Think before you key; one message, one purpose; repeat back critical orders. After METHANE, send structured updates (e.g., CAN: Conditions, Actions, Needs) every 10–15 minutes or when anything big changes.

clinicalPearls: First-in doesn't get sucked in: command, recon, report — patients come next.
Say the words 'MASS CASUALTY INCIDENT' / 'MAJOR INCIDENT DECLARED' on the radio. Ambiguity delays the cavalry.
Give casualty numbers as estimates with severity split — 'approximately' is a perfectly good word.
Your ambulance is a landmark: park it where it can serve as a visible command point without blocking the ambulance loop.
Name the staging/rendezvous point in your first report so incoming units don't self-dispatch into the scene.
redFlags: Multiple casualties down with no obvious trauma → think chemical; stop, withdraw upwind, report (Step 1-2-3).
A second explosion, gunfire, or suspicious packages → secondary-device/hostile threat; stage away.
No one has said 'I am command' within the first minutes.
Radio traffic chaos: every unit talking, no named incident, codes being used.
commonMistakes: First crew starting CPR or packaging the first patient.
Waiting for exact numbers before sending METHANE.
Forgetting the 'H' (hazards) and 'A' (access) — incoming units drive into danger or gridlock.
Parking in the hazard zone or blocking the only access road.
memoryAids: CSCATTT: 'Can Some Cops And Teachers Train Together?' — CSCA = manage, TTT = medical.
METHANE: Major — Exact location — Type — Hazards — Access — Number — Emergency services.

decisionTrees.title: First-Due Crew: First 3 Minutes
decisionTrees.content:
Approach
  → Stop short, upwind/uphill, out of traffic; look for CBRNE/violence clues
     → Clues present: withdraw, report, wait for specialist teams
     → Scene appears safe:
        Crew member 1 (COMMAND): announce arrival + 'MCI declared' + name incident
           → METHANE report → request resources → name staging
        Crew member 2 (RECON/TRIAGE): 360° look + global sort (walk/wave)
           → feed numbers back to command
  → Hand over roles (triage/treatment/transport) as units arrive

references: MIMMS (Major Incident Medical Management and Support) — CSCATTT
